site.intro: Here's what I've been building this year, including a multiplayer prediction market game, research tools, and a relaxing map of parking tickets in Los Angeles.

projects.name: Fantasy Reality
projects.one: A fantasy league, but for prediction markets.
projects.description: You join a league with friends, get a weekly allowance of fake money, and bet it on real Kalshi and Polymarket markets. Whoever calls the future best wins the season. There are parlays, achievements, AI players you can compete against, a weekly email recap, and a Discord bot that bugs the league when nobody has bet yet. It started as a weekend project on Replit and turned into the thing most of the other projects here spun out of.
projects.notes: The bug that bit me most: the season is the economy, and a league is just a group of people playing in it.

projects.name: DegenBench
projects.one: AI models bet on real markets every day. Which one is best at predicting the future?
stack: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI SDKs
projects.description: Every morning a handful of frontier models get the same set of Kalshi markets and go research them. Each one makes a forecast and explains itself. Then they all read each other's arguments (anonymized), argue back, and place a final bet from a fake bankroll. I score them on how well calibrated they are, with the market's own price as the bar to beat, and on plain profit, because that's what everyone actually wants to know.
projects.notes: Fake money only. No real orders get placed.

projects.name: Kalshi Mention Tracker
projects.one: How often does Trump actually say "tariff"? Look it up before you bet.
projects.description: Kalshi runs markets on whether someone will say a specific word during a speech or an earnings call. This tracks all of them. Search a phrase, see how often it came up at past events, and check the timeline before you put money down. I built the first version in Lovable in an afternoon, then folded it into Fantasy Reality, where it feeds the research behind the newsletter.

projects.name: Fantasy Reality Newsletter
projects.one: A newsletter about prediction markets, and the chart tool I made for it.
projects.description: Fantasy Reality is a Substack about what prediction markets are saying about reality, and what reality is saying back. The chart maker is the tool behind it: paste a Kalshi link, pick a time window, drop in some callouts, and it makes a chart in the house style. There's a straight editorial look and a louder meme version with pixel speech bubbles.
projects.notes: There's also a half-built pipeline for turning market stories into short videos. One episode in.

projects.name: Emberfall
projects.one: Play a cooperative Lord of the Rings board game with friends who live far away.
projects.description: A browser version of Fate of the Fellowship for two to five people. Someone hosts, shares a four-letter code, and everyone jumps in. The game only lets you make legal moves, every card and location explains itself when you hover, and dice rolls pause so people can spend resources before the result locks in. If you refresh, you land back in your seat with the log intact.
projects.notes: Rules are paraphrased from the rulebook. No art or card text is copied, and I'm not affiliated with anyone. Buy the real game, it's great.

projects.name: Music for Parking
projects.one: A relaxing map of parking tickets in Los Angeles.
projects.description: Real LA parking citations replayed on a map, hour by hour, and turned into music. Every ticket is a note. Different neighborhoods get their own rhythm, so the whole city becomes a slow, generative score. It's the piece I kept from a much bigger idea: a territory game played on a real hex map of LA, powered by the city's open data. The game part is still sitting in the repo.

projects.name: Sex House Island
projects.one: A fake reality show, and a playable point-and-click adventure set on the island.
projects.description: The site is a promo page for a reality show that doesn't exist: eight cast members, an island, prediction markets on who gets voted off, and an investor page. The game is the real experiment: a LucasArts-style point-and-click adventure built from scratch in TypeScript. Nine verbs, an inventory, a parrot you can talk to, and a puzzle to get into the tavern. Launch goes to the show's site. Play the game opens the adventure.
projects.notes: What I learned: the engine is the easy part. The art is the hard part.

projects.name: Gizzard Hours
projects.one: How much King Gizzard have I actually listened to?
projects.description: I exported my YouTube history and found out. Google hands you a 67 MB HTML file with no line breaks, so the first job was reading it without choking. Then: match every play to the band's 265 releases using MusicBrainz, add up listening time by month and by album, and score the albums by how heavy they are. Then do the same for the Disney catalog, for comparison. This turned into an essay on the newsletter.

projects.name: Pre-Speech Odds vs. Reality
projects.one: Does anyone know what Trump will say before he says it?
projects.description: Fifteen months of Kalshi markets on what Trump would say in his speeches, checked against every price, trade, and transcript. I worked out when each speech started by watching for the moment a word's contract snapped to 99 cents. The short version: the crowd overpays for coin flips, ignores how often he actually says things, and keeps betting on words he has dropped. And no, there's no sign of insiders.

projects.name: Chameleon Resume
projects.one: Paste a job posting and my resume tells you if I'm a fit.
projects.description: A resume that adjusts to whoever is reading it. Drop in a job posting URL and it reads the role, scores how well I match, and reorders itself to lead with the relevant stuff. Or skip that part and read it like a normal resume.
projects.notes: Built in Lovable, so it's the one thing here without a code link.
